comment.value: The manuscript investigates the problem of task-incremental learning for image restoration. To this end, the manuscript introduces a lightweight framework built around a meta-convolution module that substitutes standard convolutions in existing backbones. The proposed module leverages task-specific embedding pools to obtain hard parameter isolation. The proposed design introduces negligible computational overhead at inference, while enabling near-forgetting-free incremental learning. The manuscript received ratings of four borderline accept. Reviewers appreciated the problem setting (addressing the gap between one-by-one and all-in-one paradigms), effectiveness of the proposed design, plug-and-play design compatibility with existing image restoration backbones, and extensive experiments  (e.g., deraining, dehazing, deblurring, etc.).  Reviewers also raised several questions including, task scalability and comparison with prompt-based continual learning methods. Post-rebuttal, reviewers maintained their positive rating with reviewers mentioning that most of the concerns are addressed. Given that all reviewers are positive, rebuttal from the authors, and author-reviewer discussions, the recommendation is accept.

Thank you very much for your prompt response and thorough review. We must commend you on your careful and responsible evaluation, which has pointed out a potentially misleading aspect of our paper. Please allow us to further clarify the issue:

(1) We must admit that Figure 1(b) in the paper indeed introduces ambiguity. What we intended to represent by “multi-head” was actually those approaches that run all sub-models simultaneously during a single forward pass and then select or weight their outputs—such as Mixture-of-Experts methods. In other words, the “selective mechanism” should be placed on the output side. However, in Figure 1(b), we mistakenly drew it on the input side, which can easily lead to misunderstanding. We sincerely thank you for identifying this issue, and we will correct the figure and explain it clearly in the revised version of the paper.

(2) In fact, the paradigm illustrated in Figure 1(b) is closer to what you referred to as the “query-to-model” paradigm, where a degradation-specific query mechanism is used to select the corresponding sub-model for image restoration. We have already discussed the drawbacks of this paradigm in the section “For weakness 2.”

In summary, we believe your concerns are very valid, as Figure 1(b) indeed failed to convey our intended meaning. This was an unfortunate illustration error. We are grateful for your indirect reminder, and we will make sure to clearly distinguish between these two paradigms in the revised version and clarify the differences between the “query-to-model” paradigm and our proposed MINI.

First of all, I would like to thank the authors for their kind and detailed responses, which have resolved most of my concerns. I do, however, have a couple of follow-up questions:

In the first paragraph of your response to Weakness 1, and in your response to Weakness 2, there seems to be a potential contradiction. Specifically, the sentence "Although the 'query-to-model' approach also achieves parameter isolation and does not introduce additional inference overhead, it intuitively resembles a multi-head architecture." appears to conflict with your earlier claim that multi-head methods incur a linear increase in intermediate features and computational cost. Could you clarify this point?

In your rebuttal to Weakness 1, you mention that the number of intermediate features grows linearly with the number of tasks in multi-head methods. However, based on Figure 1-(b), it appears that only one head is activated per input during inference. Therefore, the intermediate feature size and runtime memory usage should remain constant, rather than scaling with the number of tasks.

Could you elaborate on this point in more detail? It is still somewhat unclear to me why the proposed method is considered significantly more efficient than conventional multi-head approaches in terms of computation. The claim regarding superior efficiency over existing multi-head architectures does not fully resonate with me yet.

$\textbf{Thank you very much for your thoughtful feedback}$. We fully understand your concerns, and we would like to further clarify the motivation behind our experimental design.

First, regarding your Question (1) in the comment, the answer is "yes".

Then, for Question (2), we would like to clarify as follows:

(1) The motivation behind MINI is to tackle the problem of task-incremental learning in image restoration, which inherently requires identifying “new” and “old” tasks. This makes it necessary to know task identities during training; otherwise, task-incremental learning cannot be realized. In other words, degradation supervision must be introduced during training.

(2) Based on this, we fully acknowledge that, compared to joint learning, task-incremental learning indeed introduces additional supervision (i.e., degradation labels). However, this difference arises from the nature of the task itself. Then why do we still compare the two in Table 2? Because our goal is to demonstrate that $\textbf{MINI effectively equips existing methods with strong task-incremental learning capabilities}$. As is widely recognized, joint training often serves as the upper bound of incremental learning performance. If these baselines were trained incrementally without MINI, their performance would likely degrade significantly. Yet, Table 2 shows that when equipped with MINI, their incremental performance can be comparable to joint training, which highlights MINI's effectiveness.

(3) In simpler terms, our purpose is $\textbf{not to "claim SOTA"}$, but rather to show that $\textbf{“MINI works well for incremental learning”}$. The results from joint training merely serve as a reference baseline.

We hope this addresses your concern. If you still have further questions, we are more than happy to continue the discussion.

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely appreciate your thorough review and insightful comments. We will make every effort to address all of your concerns and questions.

$\textbf{For weakness 1:}$

As we stated in the Introduction (lines 37–41), although multi-head methods achieve complete parameter isolation across tasks, their computational cost (FLOPs), number of parameters, and the amount of intermediate features grow linearly with the number of tasks. This ultimately results in a linear increase in inference time and a significant rise in computational resource consumption, which is often unacceptable in real-world applications.

In contrast, our proposed MINI maintains constant FLOPs and the amount of intermediate features regardless of the number of tasks, meaning that the inference time remains unchanged as new tasks are added. Although the number of model parameters still grows linearly with the number of tasks, it is well known that the majority of GPU memory consumption in modern deep models is dominated by the storage of intermediate features, while model parameters occupy only a small fraction of the memory. Therefore, we believe that the slight increase in memory usage brought by MINI is a worthwhile trade-off for achieving near “no-forgetting” performance in incremental learning.

$\textbf{For weakness 2:}$

We are glad that this question was raised, as the “query-to-model” approach you mentioned was indeed considered during the early stages of our research and partly inspired the development of MINI! Below, we provide a detailed explanation of the differences between this strategy and our proposed MINI:

(1) Although the "query-to-model" approach also achieves parameter isolation and does not introduce additional inference overhead, it intuitively resembles a multi-head architecture. As a result, the overall pipeline becomes less elegant, which goes against our minimalist design philosophy.

(2) Although the "query-to-model" strategy enables complete isolation of all parameter components, as we discussed in the Discussion section (lines 242–249), it is in fact unnecessary to strictly isolate non-convolutional components (e.g., LayerNorm) whose learnable parameters have minimal impact on incremental learning performance. Replacing these components with task embeddings may not introduce a large number of additional parameters, but it would make the overall architecture less streamlined and violate our minimalist design principles.

(3) In most practical applications, image restoration—being a low-level vision task—typically serves as a single functional module within a larger system (e.g., autonomous driving), providing high-quality inputs for subsequent high-level tasks such as object detection or semantic segmentation. In such scenarios, practitioners often prefer to use a single model, like our proposed MINI, to accomplish this functional block. This approach facilitates more efficient system management and optimization, rather than deploying multiple sub-models within a single functional module. Similarly, for scenarios where the algorithm needs to be deployed on edge devices (e.g., smartphones), deploying a single “one-for-all” model at once is a more practical choice compared to deploying multiple sub-models, as it better aligns with real-world engineering considerations.

Overall, we ultimately chose to design the MINI architecture and abandon the “query-to-model” approach out of considerations for algorithmic simplicity and engineering practicality. At the same time, we believe that the minimalistic nature of MINI also facilitates future improvements and upgrades based on this framework.

$\textbf{For weakness 3:}$

In our early experiments, we attempted to build the degradation classifier using either a single MLP or a series of MLPs in sequence. However, we found that the classifier consistently struggled to distinguish certain types of degradations, such as blur and fog. To address this issue, we proposed a two-stage degradation classification mechanism — performing coarse classification first, followed by fine-grained classification — which led to the design of our current query module. This simple yet effective change improved the classification accuracy by approximately 15%.

We will include the above content in Section 3.2 of the revised version to better clarify our design motivation, and we will also add an ablation study of the query module in Section 4.2. The detailed results are as follows:

|  method  | degration classify acc.|
|------|----------|
| Sequential MLPs |     78.3%     |
| Our query module |     94.6%     |

It is worth noting that the Sequential MLP maintains approximately the same number of parameters as our query module.

$\textbf{For weakness 4:}$

The parameter counts of the all-in-one baseline methods listed in Table 2 are as follows:

AirNet 8.93M

PromptIR 36M

MAXIM 14.1M

NAFNet 19.3M

Restormer 26.09M

IR-SDE-Unet 137.14M

DA-CLIP-Unet 137.14M

The corresponding MINI versions are constructed by setting the number of task-specific branches to $T=5$ in our experiments. As a result, the total parameter count of each MINI-based variant is approximately $T$ times that of its original backbone. Our lightweight query module contains only 0.11M parameters, with an inference time of few millisecond on an NVIDIA 2080Ti GPU.

$\textbf{For weakness 5:}$

Thank you for your careful reading and valuable suggestions. In the revised version, we will thoroughly review and correct all typos. As you suggested, we will also change the bold fonts in Tables 2 and 3 to red highlights to improve readability for the readers.

Thank you for your thoughtful review of our work. We will do our best to address your questions and concerns.

$\textbf{For weakness 1:}$

The core motivation behind the design of MINI is to address parameter interference across different tasks through hard isolation, thereby enabling strong incremental learning capabilities within a known set of tasks—especially under imbalanced training data conditions. The scenario you mentioned, involving an unknown number of tasks, actually falls under a much more challenging setting: open-ended incremental learning, which is not the primary focus of this paper. Nonetheless, it remains a practically important problem and will be one of the key directions in our future research.

$\textbf{For weakness 2:}$

Yes, this viewpoint has already been discussed in the “Limitation of MINI” section. However, we believe that this trade-off is entirely acceptable compared to the benefits brought by MINI—achieving nearly forgetting-free incremental learning with almost no additional computational cost. Moreover, for most models, the majority of GPU memory consumption comes from the size and number of intermediate feature maps, with only a small portion attributed to model parameters themselves. 

For example, the well-known ResNet50 [1] has only 25.6M parameters (approximately 100MB of memory in fp32), yet when training with 224×224 images and a batch size of 32, the total GPU memory usage reaches around 1.5–2GB. This indicates that the vast majority of memory is used to store intermediate features (around 95%), and this proportion increases further as the input image resolution grows. 

$\textbf{For weakness 3:}$

We are pleased to see that most reviewers seem interested in the potential extension of MINI to transformer-based architectures. Therefore, in the revised version, we will apply MINI to a representative transformer-based image restoration method, SwinIR [2], and include the experimental comparison results in the appendix (due to the limited space in the main paper). This will help evaluate the scalability of MINI within transformer-based frameworks. We are currently conducting related experiments. If you remain interested during the rebuttal phase, we would be happy to share the experimental results with you.

$\textbf{For question 1:}$

(1) In practical deployment scenarios, if the embedding pool needs to be extended to accommodate new tasks after the model has already been deployed, this can be easily implemented at the code level. For example, if we want to extend a trained MINI-based model from $T=5$ to $T=7$ tasks, we only need to initialize a $T=7$ model and load the pretrained weights for the first 5 embeddings. This can typically be achieved with a simple line of code:

model.load_state_dict(state_dict, $\textbf{strict=False}$).

Subsequently, the newly added embeddings can be trained while keeping the existing ones fixed.

(2) Since the setting of $T$ does not affect the inference-time computational cost, we only need to consider the choice of the main model and the number of tasks. For scenarios where the number of tasks is uncertain, we recommend setting a relatively large $T$ (within the limits of hardware capacity) to accommodate potential future tasks. In contrast, if the number of tasks is relatively fixed, $T$ can simply be set to the required number of tasks.

$\textbf{For question 2:}$

The issue you raised is a common challenge in the field of image restoration—how to improve the model's out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness for better generalization to complex real-world scenarios. As a plug-and-play method, MINI is designed to enhance the incremental learning capability of the backbone model. Therefore, its generalization ability largely depends on the architecture, capacity, and training strategy of the backbone itself. Therefore, we believe that the OOD robustness of MINI mainly depends on the training strategies used when learning each individual embedding (e.g., regularization), as well as the inherent generalization ability of the backbone model.

$\textbf{For question 3:}$

Same as response to $\textbf{For Weakness 3}$.

[2] SwinIR: Image Restoration Using Swin Transformer, ICCV 2021

Thank you for your careful reading and positive feedback on our work. We will address your questions thoroughly to resolve your concerns.

$\textbf{For weakness 1:}$

Indeed, as discussed in the “Limitations of MINI” section of the Discussion, the current MINI framework is designed to address incremental learning with a limited number of tasks. Open-ended incremental learning is a more challenging problem and be the focus of our future work. Nevertheless, we believe that the proposed MINI architecture remains a pioneering and practically meaningful contribution to the current research on incremental learning in the field of image restoration. Since research on incremental learning in the field of multi-task image restoration is still very limited, MINI serves as a ready-to-use solution that can be easily integrated into existing image restoration methods to effectively enhance their incremental learning capabilities. At the same time, it can also serve as a heuristic approach to inspire future researchers and provide useful insights for further exploration in incremental learning for image restoration.

$\textbf{For weakness 2:}$

(1) Completely eliminating degradation classification errors is a highly challenging task. In fact, even the state-of-the-art degradation classifier DA-CLIP [1] still exhibits around a 2% error rate. Further reducing this error typically requires significantly larger network architectures, which in turn introduces substantial additional computational cost. In this context, our proposed ECR offers a highly cost-effective solution, enabling us to maintain robust overall performance (as shown in Figures 4 and 5) while using only a lightweight degradation classifier.

(2) The original intention of MINI is to address the problem of incremental learning in multi-task image restoration, rather than to solve all-in-one image restoration under complex mixed degradation scenarios. Therefore, the query module is not specifically designed for handling mixed degradations. Moreover, whether models trained on single-degradation datasets can generalize well to mixed-degradation cases remains a challenging open problem in the image restoration community. This issue is more related to model design or training strategy optimization, rather than the core incremental learning problem that this paper focuses on.

$\textbf{For weakness 3:}$

Thank you for your valuable suggestion. In our revised version, we will include an additional evaluation in the supplementary materials to assess the impact of non-convolutional components on the final incremental learning performance. Similarly, we conducted experiments on five tasks (deraining, dehazing, raindrop removal, deblurring, and low-light enhancement) under the same training setup. The detailed experimental results are as follows:

| Method       | ave PSNR ↑ | ave SSIM ↑ | ave LPIPS ↓ |
|------------|--------|--------|--------|
| Fully embedded   | 28.844  | 0.915  | 0.0629 |
| Only MINI-conv | 28.754  | 0.911  | 0.0632 |


It can be seen that, the average performance improvement was only around 0.1 dB in PSNR. We believe this is because these parameters primarily perform affine and scaling transformations among features, and such transformations tend to exhibit limited variation across tasks within the same network architecture. Therefore, even without explicit parameter isolation, these components do not lead to severe catastrophic forgetting.

$\textbf{For weakness 4:}$

In fact, we have already included comparison results with PromptIR in Table 2, as it is a well-established all-in-one image restoration method. In addition, we compared our approach with several more recent and advanced image restoration methods, such as DA-CLIP [1] and IR-SDE [2]. The results demonstrate that MINI consistently improves the overall performance of these methods.

The methods you mentioned, L2P [3] and DualPrompt [4], are incremental learning approaches based on transformer architectures, whereas our MINI is currently designed for CNN-based architectures. Therefore, it is unfortunately not feasible to conduct comparison experiments under the same backbone. Nevertheless, we still compared the MINI-based NAFNet with the models reported in the original papers of these two methods as a reference. Similarly, we conducted comparison experiments on the five tasks considered in this paper, and the results are as follows:

| Method       | ave PSNR ↑ | ave SSIM ↑ | ave LPIPS ↓ |
|------------|--------|--------|--------|
| L2P [3] | 22.067  | 0.812  | 0.117 |
| DualPrompt [4] | 21.897  | 0.795  | 0.124 |
| MINI | 28.754  | 0.911  | 0.0632 |

The incremental training order is (rain → haze → blur → raindrop → low light). It can be clearly observed that, thanks to our hard parameter isolation design, our MINI achieves significantly better final performance. Following your suggestion, we will incorporate the comparison results with the aforementioned transformer-based incremental learning methods into Table 3.

$\textbf{For question 1:}$

MINI is specifically designed to effectively address the problem of parameter interference in multi-task image restoration. As discussed in the Discussion section, it requires predefining the maximum number of tasks $T$. In contrast, open-ended incremental learning presents a much greater challenge. Within the MINI framework, supporting such a setting would likely require a dynamically adjustable embedding pool. Based on insights from previous studies, such dynamic adjustments often necessitate the introduction of additional subnetworks (e.g., Dynamic Convolution [1]), which inevitably increases computational overhead. If such subnetworks are extensively integrated into the model, the additional cost becomes non-negligible, violating MINI’s original design goal of lightweight efficiency. Furthermore, the inclusion of such subnetworks would break the “hard parameter isolation” principle that MINI is built upon. Therefore, it is important to clarify that MINI is designed specifically for incremental learning in a fixed-task setting, rather than in open-ended scenarios.

$\textbf{For question 2:}$

This is a very interesting and insightful suggestion—to extend the current single-task classification-based query module to a multi-task weighting mechanism, thereby generalizing MINI’s single-degradation restoration capability to handle mixed degradations. However, it is important to clarify that MINI is designed to address the functional challenge of incremental learning in multi-task image restoration, rather than the performance-oriented problem of restoring images with mixed degradations. That said, as per your suggestion, we will include experimental results on the RainCityscapes dataset in the supplementary materials of our revised version, in order to clearly communicate the scope and limitations of MINI to readers.

$\textbf{For question 3:}$

The response and supplementary experimental results can be found in the section "$\textbf{For weakness 3}$".

$\textbf{For question 4:}$

(1) In fact, we have already integrated MINI into Restormer [6] and further improved its multi-task performance, as shown in Table 2. Although Restormer draws inspiration from the self-attention mechanism in transformer architectures, its core components are still convolutional layers. Therefore, the current MINI can be directly applied in a plug-and-play manner.

(2) As mentioned in the Discussion section, extending MINI to transformer-based architectures is a key direction for our future research. In theory, task specialization of simple structures such as MLPs and multi-head self-attention (MHSA) can be achieved by properly handling the computation logic between embeddings and features. However, it is important to note that in practice, the initialization of embedding parameters plays a critical role—it can significantly affect both training efficiency and final performance. Each embedding should be initialized in a way that closely aligns with the module it is intended to replace (e.g., convolution, MLP, etc.). This sometimes requires manual modification of the initialization logic in PyTorch’s $nn.Embedding$ implementation.

$\textbf{For question 5:}$

As you suggested, we will include experimental comparisons with L2P and DualPrompt in Table 3 of the revised version. The response and supplementary experimental results can be found in the section "$\textbf{For weakness 4}$".

Thank you very much for your recognition and positive feedback on our work. Your response is truly encouraging to us. We will carefully and thoroughly address your questions to resolve your concerns.

$\textbf{For question 1:}$

As you mentioned, Dynamic Conv and PromptIR share certain similarities with our proposed MINI. In fact, during the early stages of our investigation into incremental learning for image restoration, we conducted an in-depth study of the design principles behind these two methods to assess their potential benefits. However, we ultimately found that both approaches have certain inherent limitations that are difficult to overcome, which in turn inspired us to design MINI.

(1) Dynamic convolution methods such as Dynamic Convolution and MetaConv introduce additional subnetworks to generate adaptive convolution kernels based on the input, thereby partially alleviating the issue of parameter conflict. However, as discussed in the Introduction (lines 46–51), replacing a large portion of the original backbone with such dynamic convolutions incurs considerable computational overhead. Moreover, these methods do not explicitly isolate task-specific parameters at the architectural level. Instead, they rely on the model to “implicitly” learn task differentiation during training, which is often difficult to optimize and inherently uncertain in practice. In contrast, our MINIconv does not require the introduction of additional subnetworks, thus avoiding extra computational overhead. This enables it to replace a large number of standard convolution units in the backbone, leading to more effective parameter isolation. Moreover, we enforce hard parameter isolation directly at the architectural level, which is not only effective but also highly optimization-friendly. To highlight these advantages, we will add a comparison with Dynamic Convolution methods in terms of performance, FLOPs, and Params in Section 4.1.

(2) PromptIR, as a representative prompt/prior-based all-in-one method (as illustrated in Figure 1(a)), typically introduces learnable parameter components (Prompt Blocks) into the main network to guide the model in adapting to multiple tasks. While this strategy can enhance multi-task performance to some extent, it does not address the issue of parameter interference within the main network, thus leading to performance bottlenecks. In contrast, MINI explicitly addresses this issue by replacing standard convolutions in the main network with MINIconv, thereby further improving multi-task performance. In fact, as shown in Table 2, integrating MINIconv into the main network of PromptIR significantly boosts its performance and also equips it with incremental learning capability.

$\textbf{For question 2:}$

These all-in-one methods typically rely on different task data to “implicitly” learn degradation type classification during training, and subsequently learn how to perform restoration. In contrast, MINI adopts an incremental learning paradigm that decouples these two steps: we explicitly train task-specific embeddings for each task, and then train a lightweight query module to perform degradation classification. 

Our core motivation is to achieve parameter isolation across different tasks. Therefore, during the embedding training phase, we intentionally train embeddings for different tasks separately and explicitly. It is important to emphasize that the performance improvement should not be attributed solely to the change in training strategy, but rather to the structural parameter isolation enabled by our design.

$\textbf{For question 3:}$

Our goal is to design a plug-and-play, general-purpose multi-task incremental learning paradigm, which requires us to introduce as little additional computational overhead as possible into the original model. In the MINI architecture, the only extra computation comes from the degradation classifier, so we are very cautious in selecting its design.

(1) The approach in DCPT, which uses the decoder as a degradation classifier to enhance the encoder’s multi-task capability, is indeed elegant. However, such a design goes against our minimalist philosophy. First, training the DCPT decoder requires intermediate features from the restoration model (encoder) as input. Yet, different models have different feature resolutions in their intermediate layers, making it difficult to deploy a DCPT-style decoder in a plug-and-play manner across various architectures. Additionally, it introduces considerable computational overhead. In contrast, our proposed query module is structurally independent of the main network and achieves effective degradation classification with minimal computational cost. We will include a detailed comparison with DCPT in Section 4.1 and evaluate whether a MINI-based variant of DCPT can achieve even better performance.

(2) Misclassification by the degradation classifier is almost inevitable. To minimize its impact on the final performance, we propose the Embedding-Consistency Regularization (ECR) strategy (Section 3.3). Its effectiveness is demonstrated in the ablation study (Figures 4 and 5 in Section 4.2). The results show that ECR significantly improves the model’s robustness under misclassification scenarios.

$\textbf{For question 4:}$

This is indeed an interesting observation. A model with complete parameter isolation should, in theory, achieve consistent performance regardless of the training order. Although our MINI achieves near-complete parameter isolation, as discussed in Section 5 (Discussion), most baseline architectures still contain a small number of shared parameter components beyond standard convolutions—such as LayerNorm and nn.Parameter elements—which may introduce minor parameter conflict. This residual overlap is the primary reason behind the slight performance differences observed under different training orders. However, we found in practice that these shared parameters rarely lead to catastrophic forgetting. Therefore, in favor of architectural simplicity, we did not propose replacements like “MINI-LayerNorm” to fully isolate these components.

We will address this point in our revised version. Specifically, we will add an explanatory note at line 239 to clarify this issue.

$\textbf{For question 5:}$

As you pointed out, selecting appropriate numbers of training iterations based on the scale of each dataset can indeed further improve the final performance. We are happy to explore this in future work. In this paper, however, our primary focus is on the comparison between models before and after applying MINI (Table 2), rather than on performance optimization. Therefore, we adopted a unified number of training epochs across tasks as a rough setting to validate the improvements brought by MINI in both multi-task and incremental learning scenarios.

$\textbf{For question 6:}$

As mentioned in the Discussion section, our future work will extend MINI to transformer-based architectures. We also hope that our work can inspire future researchers to design interesting modules such as “MINI-MLP” or “MINI-Transformer” etc.

$\textbf{For question 7:}$

This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed MINI on five common image restoration tasks. However, this does not imply that MINI's generalizability is limited to these five tasks. With appropriate settings of the task ID (T) values, MINI can also be applied to other image restoration tasks (e.g., glare removal, image denoising, etc.) with only minimal impact on previously learned tasks.

As a plug-and-play approach, the generalization ability of MINI largely depends on that of the underlying backbone model. Therefore, it is difficult to evaluate the generalization of MINI in isolation. The design of MINI aims to enhance the task-incremental and multi-task capabilities of existing methods.

$\textbf{For Paper Formatting Concerns:}$

Thank you for your suggestion. We will revise the description in Section 4 by separating the experimental setup into a standalone subsection.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The outstanding contribution of this article is the introduction of incremental learning for image restoration tasks. I will mainly list here what I think are the weaknesses of this paper:

1. The MINI-Conv is very similar to the Dynamic Conv [1] and also the Prompt Block in PromptIR [2]. Perhaps the authors could discuss the difference between these two?
2. I am quite confused by the comparative experimental setup of this paper. Taking Table 2 as an example, this paper compares the all-in-one (joint learning) method with the incremental learning-based method. The all-in-one method trains on five degradation jointly, and the training process is blind. However, the incremental learning based method proposed in this paper can get the correct degradation type embedding during training, which is not blind. Will this difference affect the final restoration performance?
3. Why not use the image restoration network itself as the degradation classifier, such as DCPT [3]? Is an external degradation classifier necessary? As I understand, MINI-Conv requires additional degradation classification during inference. If the degradation classification result is wrong, can the MINI-Conv-based method still output a clean image?
4. I am very interested in the ablation experiment results of the Task sequence order. Why do different Task sequence orders lead to different results? The PSNR difference between 1→2→3→4→5 and 1→3→2→5→4 is 0.2 dB, which cannot be called "little impact".
5. Does the data imbalance problem affect the effect of incremental learning? I noticed that the proposed method trains 400 epochs for each dataset. If this training epoch is redistributed according to the actual data volume of the dataset, can better results be achieved? For example, train more epochs for the small dataset (LoL) and train fewer epochs for the large dataset (RESIDE).
6. For networks that do not use convolution, such as SwinIR, is MINI-Conv still useful?
7. Is MINI-Conv applicable to mixed degradation or more degradation types? Can MINI-Conv be generalized to real degradation scenarios?

[1] Dynamic Convolution: Attention over Convolution Kernels. CVPR 2020.

[2] PromptIR: Prompting for All-in-One Blind Image Restoration. NeurIPS 2023.

[3] DCPT: Universal Image Restoration Pre-training via Degradation Classification. ICLR 2025.

summary.value: This paper addresses the challenge of task-incremental learning for image restoration, where models struggle to sequentially add new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. The authors propose a lightweight framework MINI built around MINIconv, a novel meta-convolution module that replaces standard convolutions in existing backbones. MINIconv uses task-specific embedding pools to achieve hard parameter isolation: each task exclusively activates its own embeddings during inference, preventing interference with prior tasks. This design requires no complex meta-networks, introduces negligible computational overhead during inference, and enables near-forgetting-free incremental learning.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. This paper systematically address task-incremental learning for image restoration (IR), filling a critical gap between "one-by-one" and "all-in-one" paradigms.
2. MINI mechanism replaces complex meta-networks with lightweight embedding pools, achieving hard parameter isolation without inference overhead. The design is simple yet effective.
3. Plug-and-play compatibility with existing IR backbones (e.g., NAFNet, Restormer) significantly boosts practicality. Experiments show consistent multi-task performance gains.
4. Extensive experiments across 5 diverse IR tasks (deraining, dehazing, deblurring, etc.) using multiple backbones.

Weakness:
1. Potential limited task scalability: The fixed embedding pool size T requires predefining the maximum number of tasks, which may be impractical for open-ended incremental learning.
2. Despite ECR, performance still depends on the query module’s accuracy. The paper reports a 6% misclassification rate, and ECR only mitigates, not eliminates errors. Meanwhile, the lightweight query design (global/local branches) may struggle with complex hybrid degradations (e.g., rainy + hazy images).
3. Non-convolutional components (e.g., LayerNorm) are not adapted to MINI’s isolation paradigm. The authors note this has "limited impact," but no data supports this claim.
4. For experiments, this paper lacks comparison against prompt-based continual learning methods (e.g., L2P, DualPrompt), which also tackle task-incremental settings. The "all-in-one" joint training baselines (Table 2) are not state-of-the-art (e.g., missing recent works like PromptIR).

questions.value:
1. How would MINI scale to open-ended task sequences (e.g., >10 tasks) without retraining? Could you propose strategies (e.g., embedding pruning/generation) to dynamically expand capacity while preserving efficiency?
2. How does MINI handle hybrid degradations (e.g., rainy + hazy images)? Could you test on blended datasets (e.g., RainCityscapes) or modify the query for multi-label classification?
3. Could you ablate MINI’s performance when these layers are made task-specific versus shared? Would adapting them (e.g., via embeddings) further boost multi-task gains?
4. Can MINIConv integrate into transformer backbones (e.g., Restormer)? Does replacing MHSA/MLP weights with embeddings require architectural changes? Please discuss feasibility.
5. Why omit comparisons against prompt-based continual learning (e.g., L2P, DualPrompt) that also tackle task-incremental settings? Could you add these to Table 3 to clarify MINI’s advantages over parameter-efficient alternatives?

limitations.value: Please see the Weakness and Question parts.

summary.value: The paper proposes MINI, a minimalistic framework for task-incremental learning in image restoration, addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting and parameter conflict in existing multi-task models. MINI introduces a novel Meta Convolution module (MINIconv) that generates task-specific parameters via lightweight embedding pools, enabling complete parameter isolation across tasks without additional computational overhead. This design allows seamless integration into existing backbones, transforming them into incremental learning systems. A degradation query mechanism classifies input degradations to select appropriate embeddings, while embedding-consistency regularization enhances robustness against misclassification.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1.This work represents the first systematic attempt to explore task-incremental learning in the field of image restoration.

2.The proposed architecture is highly minimalistic, requiring only the replacement of standard convolutional layers with MINIconv and the addition of a lightweight degradation query module. It can be seamlessly integrated into existing mainstream backbone networks.

3.The method enables efficient and nearly forgetting-free task-incremental learning, while avoiding the parameter explosion issues typical of multi-head approaches.

4.The introduction of Embedding Consistency Regularization (ECR) effectively enhances the system's robustness and fault tolerance, particularly when the degradation classification is inaccurate.
 
Weaknesses:
1.The maximum number of tasks supported is inherently constrained by the pre-defined size of the embedding pool (T), making it difficult to accommodate scenarios where the total number of tasks is unknown or grows dynamically.

2.Although the method avoids additional inference-time computation, hard parameter isolation causes the total number of model parameters to grow linearly with the number of tasks, which may present challenges for deployment in resource-constrained environments.

3.The current work primarily focuses on CNN-based architectures, and its generalization to other popular frameworks such as Vision Transformers or Diffusion Models remains unexplored.

questions.value:
Q1:The MINI architecture requires pre-defining the embedding pool size T to accommodate different tasks. However, real-world applications may face an unknown or unbounded number of tasks. Can the authors clarify whether MINI can dynamically extend T post-deployment? If not, what practical upper bound do the authors recommend for T considering memory and computational trade-offs?

Q2:The degradation query module relies on accurate task classification. While the paper discusses robustness via ECR, in practice, real-world degradation can be ambiguous or unknown. Can the authors elaborate on MINI's performance when encountering degradations outside the predefined set?

Q3:The paper mentions potential future extensions to Transformer-based backbones but lacks preliminary results or analysis. Can the authors provide insights or experiments indicating MINI's compatibility or limitations with Transformer or hybrid architectures?

summary.value: The authors propose MINI (Minimalistic Incremental Network for Image Restoration), a novel and lightweight framework tailored for task-incremental learning across various image restoration tasks. To enable effective hard parameter isolation, they introduce MINIconv, along with a lightweight degradation query module and an embedding consistency regularization (ECR) strategy.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
[Strengths]
1. This work is the first attempt to explore task-incremental learning in the field of image restoration.
2. The idea is performed well.
3. The paper is well-organized and easy to read.
4. The limitations are clearly and well mentioned.

[Weaknesses]
1. In line 258, the authors state that "its use of hard parameter isolation causes the total number of parameters to scale by a factor of T." If this is the case, isn’t there a significant difference in terms of forward computation overhead or the number of parameters compared to multi-head methods?

2. In the same context as the previous question, I am curious about the performance differences and differences in parameter counts between MINI and a scenario where a learned query function selects task-specific (one-for-one) methods for each task.

3. What is the performance when only the Degradation Classification MLP is used in the query function, excluding the Global MLP and Local MLP?

4. I am curious about the actual number of parameters in each case listed in Table 2. Additionally, what is the parameter count and inference time of the MLP-based query function? 

5. Minor error.
-- L17: overll >> overall
-- Table 2: It would be visually more effective to use color for emphasis rather than bold text.

title.value: A Minimalistic Unified Framework for Incremental Learning across Image Restoration Tasks

TLDR.value: A Minimalistic multi-task image restoration architecture based on adaptive convolutional kernels, well-suited for task-incremental learning.

abstract.value: Existing research in low-level vision has shifted its focus from "one-by-one" task-specific methods to "all-in-one" multi-task unified architectures. However, current all-in-one image restoration approaches primarily aim to improve overall performance across a limited number of tasks. In contrast, how to incrementally add new image restoration capabilities on top of an existing model — that is, task-incremental learning — has been largely unexplored. To fill this research gap, we propose a minimalistic and universal paradigm for task-incremental learning called MINI. It addresses the problem of parameter interference across different tasks through a simple yet effective mechanism, enabling nearly forgetting-free task-incremental learning. Specifically, we design a special meta-convolution called MINI-Conv, which generates parameters solely through lightweight embeddings instead of complex convolutional networks or MLPs. This not only significantly reduces the number of parameters and computational overhead but also achieves complete parameter isolation across different tasks. Moreover, MINI-Conv can be seamlessly integrated as a plug-and-play replacement for any convolutional layer within existing backbone networks, endowing them with incremental learning capabilities. Therefore, our method is highly generalizable. Finally, we demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing incremental learning approaches across five common image restoration tasks. Moreover, the near forgetting-free nature of our method makes it highly competitive even against all-in-one image restoration methods trained in a full-supervised manner. Our code is available at https://github.com.
